glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: On the night the LORD strikes Egypt’s firstborn, He shelters Israel’s households under the blood of an unblemished lamb, brings His people out after 430 years, and makes that night a memorial to be kept and explained throughout their generations.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Exodus 12 opens the fourth major movement of the book. The final plague announced in chapter 11 now falls, and the LORD gives His instructions before it does.

glance.label: Chapter Outline
glance.html:
• Exodus 12:1–13 — The LORD Gives the Passover Lamb and the Sign of the Blood

  • Exodus 12:14–20 — The Day Becomes a Memorial and the Feast of Unleavened Bread

  • Exodus 12:21–28 — Moses Instructs the Elders and Israel Worships and Obeys

  • Exodus 12:29–36 — The LORD Strikes Egypt’s Firstborn and Pharaoh Sends Israel Out

  • Exodus 12:43–51 — Who May Keep the Passover

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “Now the blood shall be a sign for you on the houses where you are. And when I see the blood, I will pass over you; and the plague shall not be on you to destroy you when I strike the land of Egypt.” (Exodus 12:13)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Before the judgment falls, God resets Israel’s calendar: “This month shall be your beginning of months” (12:2). Their year will now begin with redemption. Each household takes a lamb “without blemish” (12:5), kills it at twilight, puts its blood on the doorposts and lintel, and eats it dressed for travel. The blood is God’s appointed sign: “when I see the blood, I will pass over you” (12:13). Protection rests on the sign God gives, not on Israel’s own worthiness, and the people trust His word and obey before anything has happened.

At midnight the LORD strikes every firstborn in Egypt and executes judgment “against all the gods of Egypt” (12:12). There is not a house without a death, except where the blood is. Pharaoh, who once asked “Who is the LORD?”, now tells Israel to go and serve Him, and even asks for a blessing. A family of seventy leaves as about six hundred thousand men on foot, with their children and a mixed multitude, carrying unleavened dough in their haste.

Woven through the story are instructions for remembering it: a feast of unleavened bread, children’s questions to answer, and a Passover open to any outsider willing to join God’s people. The New Testament sees the fulfillment plainly: “Christ, our Passover, was sacrificed for us” (1 Corinthians 5:7), and not one of His bones was broken (John 19:36).

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Exodus 12:1–13 — The LORD Gives the Passover Lamb and the Sign of the Blood

The LORD makes this month the first of Israel’s year and commands each household to take an unblemished lamb, kill it at twilight, put its blood on the doorposts and lintel, and eat it in haste, ready to leave. He will strike Egypt’s firstborn and judge its gods, but He will pass over every house marked by the blood.

Exodus 12:14–20 — The Day Becomes a Memorial and the Feast of Unleavened Bread

The day is to be kept as a memorial and a feast to the LORD in every generation. For seven days Israel must remove all leaven and eat unleavened bread, with holy gatherings on the first and seventh days, because on that day the LORD brought their armies out of Egypt.

Exodus 12:21–28 — Moses Instructs the Elders and Israel Worships and Obeys

Moses tells the elders to kill the Passover lamb, apply the blood with hyssop, and stay inside until morning, for the LORD will not let the destroyer enter. When their children ask what the service means, they are to tell what the LORD did, and the people bow, worship, and obey.

Exodus 12:29–36 — The LORD Strikes Egypt’s Firstborn and Pharaoh Sends Israel Out

At midnight the LORD strikes every firstborn in Egypt, and a great cry rises in Egypt, for there is not an Egyptian house where someone is not dead. Pharaoh sends Israel out to serve the LORD, the Egyptians urge them to hurry, and the LORD gives Israel favor so that the Egyptians give them silver, gold, and clothing.

Exodus 12:37–42 — Israel Departs After 430 Years on a Night to Be Observed

About six hundred thousand men on foot, besides children, set out from Rameses with a mixed multitude and many animals, baking unleavened cakes because they left in haste. At the end of 430 years, on the very same day, the LORD’s armies go out, and the night becomes one Israel must keep for all generations.

Exodus 12:43–51 — Who May Keep the Passover

The LORD sets the terms of the Passover: no foreigner or hired worker may eat it, but a servant or stranger whose males are circumcised may keep it as one of Israel, under one law for all. It is eaten in one house without breaking a bone of the lamb, and on that same day the LORD brings Israel out of Egypt.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Exodus 12 is the heart of the exodus and one of the clearest pictures of salvation in the Old Testament. God provides the lamb, appoints the blood as the sign, and promises to pass over those who shelter under it. Jesus ate the Passover with His disciples the night before He died and gave it new meaning in His own body and blood (Matthew 26:17–29).

The chapter also shows that God wants His saving acts remembered. He builds the memory into a calendar, a meal, and the questions of children, so that every generation can say what the LORD did for them. The door to the Passover stood open to any outsider who joined the LORD’s people. From the beginning, God’s redemption was larger than one family line.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
The lamb and the blood. God provides an unblemished lamb and makes its blood the sign of protection (12:3–7, 13, 21–23).

Judgment on Egypt and its gods. The LORD strikes the firstborn and judges “all the gods of Egypt” (12:12, 29–30).

Memorial and teaching. The night is to be remembered by feast and explained to children in every generation (12:14, 24–27, 42).

Haste and readiness. Israel eats dressed to travel and leaves with unleavened dough (12:11, 34, 39).

One law for all. Outsiders may join the Passover through circumcision and share one law with the native-born (12:43–49).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Passover (12:11). The LORD’s passing over the houses marked with blood, and the meal that remembers it. Paul calls Christ “our Passover” (1 Corinthians 5:7).

Unleavened bread (12:8, 15–20). Bread made without yeast. It recalls the haste of leaving Egypt, and leaven is removed from every house for the seven days of the feast.

Hyssop (12:22). A bushy plant used to brush the blood onto the doorposts and lintel.

The destroyer (12:23). The agent of judgment that the LORD did not allow into houses marked by the blood.

Four hundred and thirty years (12:40–41). The length of Israel’s sojourn as the NKJV records it. Faithful readers differ over whether it covers Israel’s time in Egypt alone or reaches back to the promise to Abraham (compare Galatians 3:17).

Mixed multitude (12:38). Non-Israelites who left Egypt with Israel. Their presence hints at God’s welcome to outsiders, though they later became a source of complaint (Numbers 11:4).

focus: Exodus 12 records the night the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt: He gives the Passover lamb and its blood as the sign that shelters Israel’s houses, strikes Egypt’s firstborn at midnight, and leads His people out after 430 years. Instructions, events, and lasting ordinances are woven together, so that the night of rescue becomes a memorial to be kept throughout Israel’s generations.

sections.title: The LORD Gives the Passover Lamb and the Sign of the Blood
sections.summary: The LORD makes this month the first of Israel’s year and commands each household, sharing with its neighbor if it is too small, to take a lamb “without blemish” (Exodus 12:5), kill it at twilight, put its blood on the doorposts and lintel, and eat it in haste, ready to leave. He will strike Egypt’s firstborn and judge all its gods, but “when I see the blood, I will pass over you” (Exodus 12:13).

sections.title: The Day Becomes a Memorial and the Feast of Unleavened Bread
sections.summary: The day is to be a memorial kept “as a feast to the LORD throughout your generations” (Exodus 12:14). For seven days Israel is to remove leaven and eat unleavened bread, holding holy convocations on the first and seventh days, because on that day the LORD brought their armies out of Egypt.

sections.title: Moses Instructs the Elders and Israel Worships and Obeys
sections.summary: Moses tells the elders to kill the Passover lamb, apply the blood with hyssop, and stay inside until morning, for the LORD will not allow the destroyer to enter. He commands them to keep this service in the land and to answer their children’s question, and the people bow their heads, worship, and do as the LORD commanded.

sections.title: The LORD Strikes Egypt’s Firstborn and Pharaoh Sends Israel Out
sections.summary: At midnight the LORD strikes every firstborn in Egypt, and a great cry rises, “for there was not a house where there was not one dead” (Exodus 12:30). Pharaoh summons Moses and Aaron and tells them to go and serve the LORD, the Egyptians urge them to leave in haste, and the LORD gives Israel favor so that the Egyptians grant the silver, gold, and clothing they ask for.

sections.title: Israel Departs After 430 Years on a Night to Be Observed
sections.summary: About six hundred thousand men on foot, besides children, journey from Rameses to Succoth with a mixed multitude and much livestock, baking unleavened cakes because they were driven out in haste. At the end of 430 years all the armies of the LORD go out of Egypt, and the night becomes “a solemn observance for all the children of Israel throughout their generations” (Exodus 12:42).

sections.title: Who May Keep the Passover
sections.summary: The ordinance of the Passover sets who may eat it: no foreigner, sojourner, or hired servant may eat it, a bought servant may eat it once he is circumcised, and a stranger may keep it once all his males are circumcised, for “One law shall be for the native-born and for the stranger” (Exodus 12:49). It also sets how it is eaten, in one house with none of its flesh carried outside and not one of its bones broken, and Israel does as the LORD commanded, and on that same day the LORD brings them out of Egypt.

1.brief: The LORD speaks to Moses and Aaron while they are still in Egypt. The instructions that follow are given before the deliverance, so Israel must act on God’s word in advance.
1.explain:
“Now the LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, saying,”

The scene shifts from the palace to instructions for Israel. The narrator notes that God spoke “in the land of Egypt.” The Passover was given before the deliverance, while Israel was still in bondage. They had to act on God’s word before they saw it fulfilled.
1.notes: Most of Israel’s laws were given at Sinai. The Passover is the exception, given in Egypt itself, because it is bound up with the night of the exodus.

2.brief: “This month shall be your beginning of months.” God resets Israel’s calendar around the night He will redeem them, so their year begins with His act of deliverance.
2.explain:
“This month shall be your beginning of months; it shall be the first month of the year to you.”

God resets Israel’s calendar. The month of their deliverance becomes “the first month of the year.” Their year will now begin with God’s act of redemption. Every year would start by remembering how God brought them out.
2.notes: This month is later called Abib (13:4; 23:15; 34:18), meaning young ears of grain, and after the exile it was called Nisan (Nehemiah 2:1; Esther 3:7). It falls in March–April. Israel also kept a civil year beginning in the autumn, which later Judaism observed as the new year.

3.brief: On the tenth day of the month every man is to take a lamb for his father’s house, “a lamb for a household.” The Passover is centered in Israel’s homes, and verse 4 explains how small households will share a lamb with their neighbors.
3.explain:
“Speak to all the congregation of Israel, saying:”

The instructions go to “all the congregation of Israel.” This is the first time Exodus calls Israel a “congregation,” an assembled people under God.

“On the tenth of this month every man shall take for himself a lamb, according to the house of his father, a lamb for a household.”

On “the tenth” day, each family is to choose its lamb. The Passover centers in the home: “a lamb for a household.” Each family would have its own lamb, its own meal, and its own blood on the door.
3.notes: The Hebrew word translated “lamb” can refer to a young sheep or a young goat, as 12:5 makes clear.

4.brief: If a household is too small for a whole lamb, it is to share one with its nearest neighbor according to the number of persons. God makes provision so that no family is left out and none of the lamb is wasted.
4.explain:
“And if the household is too small for the lamb, let him and his neighbor next to his house take it according to the number of the persons;”

If a family is too small to eat a whole lamb, it is to join with “his neighbor next to his house.” No family is left out because it is too small.

“according to each man’s need you shall make your count for the lamb.”

The count is made by how much each person will eat. The lamb is to be eaten completely that night (12:10), so the size of the group must match the lamb. God makes provision so that no family is left out and none of the lamb is wasted.

5.brief: The lamb must be “without blemish, a male of the first year,” taken from the sheep or the goats. Only a whole, healthy animal is fit for this purpose, and the New Testament later sees Christ as the Lamb without blemish.
5.explain:
“Your lamb shall be without blemish, a male of the first year.”

The lamb must be “without blemish,” whole and healthy, with no defect. It must be “a male of the first year,” a young animal in its prime. Only the best was fit for this purpose.

“You may take it from the sheep or from the goats.”

Either a sheep or a goat was acceptable. The requirement concerned the animal’s soundness, not its kind.
5.notes: The requirement that sacrificial animals be without blemish runs through the law (Leviticus 22:19–22).

6.brief: Israel is to keep the lamb until the fourteenth day, and then the whole assembly will kill it at twilight. The entire congregation acts together at the same appointed time.
6.explain:
“Now you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of the same month.”

The family was to keep the lamb for four days, from the tenth to “the fourteenth.” During that time the lamb could be watched to confirm it had no defect.

“Then the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall kill it at twilight.”

All Israel acts together. “The whole assembly” kills the lambs at the same appointed time, “at twilight.” Though each household kills its own lamb, the whole people acts as one.
6.notes: The phrase translated “at twilight” reads literally between the two evenings. It most likely refers to the time between sunset and dark. Later Jewish practice understood it as the afternoon, from about three o’clock to sunset.

7.brief: Each household is to put some of the blood on the two doorposts and on the lintel of the houses where they eat it. The blood marks the homes of those who trust God’s word.
7.explain:
“And they shall take some of the blood and put it on the two doorposts and on the lintel of the houses where they eat it.”

The blood is to be placed on “the two doorposts” and “the lintel,” the beam over the door. Every house where the lamb is eaten must be marked. The blood marks the homes of those who trust God’s word.

8.brief: Israel is to eat the meat that night, roasted in fire, with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. The meal combines the lamb with reminders of haste and of the bitterness of slavery.
8.explain:
“Then they shall eat the flesh on that night;”

The meal is eaten “on that night,” the night of the judgment.

“roasted in fire, with unleavened bread and with bitter herbs they shall eat it.”

The lamb is “roasted in fire.” It is eaten “with unleavened bread,” bread made without yeast, which needed no time to rise, and “with bitter herbs.” The meal joins the lamb with reminders of haste and of the bitterness of slavery (1:14).
8.notes: The Hebrew word for “bitter herbs” comes from the same root as “bitter” in 1:14, “they made their lives bitter with hard bondage.”

9.brief: The lamb is not to be eaten raw or boiled but roasted whole, with its head, legs, and entrails. God directs even the manner of preparing the lamb.
9.explain:
“Do not eat it raw, nor boiled at all with water, but roasted in fire—”

The lamb must be roasted, not eaten raw or boiled.

“its head with its legs and its entrails.”

The lamb is roasted whole, cooked as one complete animal. God directs even how the lamb is prepared.

10.brief: None of the lamb may remain until morning, and anything left over must be burned. The meal belongs entirely to this one night.
10.explain:
“You shall let none of it remain until morning, and what remains of it until morning you shall burn with fire.”

Nothing is to be left over. Any remains must be burned by morning. The meal belongs to this one night, and none of the lamb would be kept for ordinary use.

11.brief: Israel is to eat dressed for travel, with belts on, sandals on their feet, and staffs in hand, eating in haste, for “It is the LORD’s Passover.” Israel eats ready to leave, trusting that God will bring them out that very night.
11.explain:
“And thus you shall eat it: with a belt on your waist, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand.”

Israel is to eat dressed for travel. A belt gathered up the long outer robe for walking. Sandals were normally removed indoors. A staff was used on a journey. Every detail says they are about to leave.

“So you shall eat it in haste.”

They are to eat “in haste,” ready to go at a moment’s notice.

“It is the LORD’s Passover.”

The meal belongs to the LORD. This is the first use of the name Passover. Israel eats ready to leave, trusting that God will bring them out that very night.
11.notes: The Hebrew word for “Passover” is “pesach,” from a verb meaning to pass over (12:13, 23, 27). Some interpreters understand the verb as protecting or hovering over, since Isaiah 31:5 uses it alongside “defending” and “preserving.”

12.brief: God declares that He will pass through Egypt that night, strike every firstborn of man and beast, and execute judgment “against all the gods of Egypt.” The final plague is God’s judgment on Egypt and its false gods.
12.explain:
“For I will pass through the land of Egypt on that night,”

God will “pass through” Egypt Himself.

“and will strike all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, both man and beast;”

The judgment announced in 11:5 will fall on “all the firstborn,” human and animal.

“and against all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgment: I am the LORD.”

The final plague is also God’s “judgment” on “all the gods of Egypt.” The plagues have shown that Egypt’s gods cannot protect it. This last blow strikes the land they were thought to guard. “I am the LORD.” He alone is God.
12.notes: Numbers 33:4 says, “Also on their gods the LORD had executed judgments.” Egypt worshiped many gods connected with the Nile, the land, the sky, and Pharaoh himself. Interpreters have linked individual plagues with particular gods. The text speaks of God’s judgment on Egypt’s gods in general, so specific links are illustrative rather than stated.

13.brief: “The blood shall be a sign for you,” and God promises, “when I see the blood, I will pass over you.” Israel’s protection rests on the sign God appointed, and 1 Corinthians 5:7 later calls Christ our Passover.
13.explain:
“Now the blood shall be a sign for you on the houses where you are.”

The blood is “a sign for you.” It marks the houses where God’s people are, and it assures them of God’s promise.

“And when I see the blood, I will pass over you;”

God gives the promise plainly. Israel’s safety did not rest on their own worth but on the blood God appointed.

“and the plague shall not be on you to destroy you when I strike the land of Egypt.”

The judgment that falls on Egypt will not touch those under the blood. Israel’s protection rests on the sign God appointed. Paul later writes, “For indeed Christ, our Passover, was sacrificed for us” (1 Corinthians 5:7). The blood of the Passover lamb, which shielded Israel from judgment, points ahead to Christ, whose blood shields His people.

14.brief: The Passover day is to be a memorial, kept as a feast to the LORD throughout their generations by an everlasting ordinance. The night of deliverance will be remembered and celebrated by every generation.
14.explain:
“So this day shall be to you a memorial;”

The day of deliverance is to be “a memorial.” It will be remembered every year.

“and you shall keep it as a feast to the LORD throughout your generations. You shall keep it as a feast by an everlasting ordinance.”

Israel is to keep it “as a feast to the LORD” in every generation, by “an everlasting ordinance.” The night of deliverance will be celebrated for all time. Jesus kept the Passover with His disciples on the night He was betrayed and gave the Lord’s Supper in that setting (Matthew 26:17–29), and Christians now remember their redemption at the Lord’s Table (1 Corinthians 11:23–26).

15.brief: For seven days they are to eat unleavened bread and remove leaven from their houses on the first day, and anyone who eats leavened bread during that time will be cut off from Israel. The Passover is joined to a week-long feast that God takes with great seriousness.
15.explain:
“Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread.”

The Passover is joined to a week-long feast of “unleavened bread.”

“On the first day you shall remove leaven from your houses.”

Every house must be cleared of leaven on the first day. Leaven was a portion of fermented dough kept from a previous batch to make new bread rise.

“For whoever eats leavened bread from the first day until the seventh day, that person shall be cut off from Israel.”

The penalty is severe. Anyone who eats leavened bread during the feast “shall be cut off from Israel.” God takes the feast with great seriousness. Paul later draws on this feast when he urges believers to purge out the old leaven and keep the feast “with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Corinthians 5:7–8).
15.notes: The phrase “cut off” means to be removed from the community of God’s people. Interpreters differ on whether it referred to death, exclusion, or judgment left in God’s hands.

16.brief: The first and seventh days are holy convocations on which no work is done except preparing food. The feast is framed by days set apart for the LORD.
16.explain:
“On the first day there shall be a holy convocation, and on the seventh day there shall be a holy convocation for you.”

The feast is framed by two holy convocations, sacred assemblies on the first and seventh days.

“No manner of work shall be done on them; but that which everyone must eat—that only may be prepared by you.”

On those days no ordinary work is allowed, except preparing food. The days are set apart for the LORD.

17.brief: Israel is to observe the Feast of Unleavened Bread because on that very day God brought their armies out of Egypt. The feast is tied directly to the day of their departure.
17.explain:
“So you shall observe the Feast of Unleavened Bread,”

The feast has its name: “the Feast of Unleavened Bread.”

“for on this same day I will have brought your armies out of the land of Egypt.”

The feast is tied to the very day of departure. God speaks of Israel’s “armies,” the people marching out in organized ranks. God speaks of the deliverance as though it were already done.

“Therefore you shall observe this day throughout your generations as an everlasting ordinance.”

Like the Passover itself, this feast is to be kept “throughout your generations.”

18.brief: Unleavened bread is to be eaten from the evening of the fourteenth day to the evening of the twenty-first. God sets the exact limits of the feast.
18.explain:
“In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month at evening, you shall eat unleavened bread, until the twenty-first day of the month at evening.”

God sets the exact limits. The feast runs from the evening of “the fourteenth day” to the evening of “the twenty-first day.” God sets the exact time of the feast.

19.brief: No leaven may be found in their houses for seven days, and whoever eats anything leavened, whether stranger or native, will be cut off from the congregation. The same law applies to everyone who belongs to Israel.
19.explain:
“For seven days no leaven shall be found in your houses,”

For the whole week, “no leaven” may be found in Israel’s houses.

“since whoever eats what is leavened, that same person shall be cut off from the congregation of Israel, whether he is a stranger or a native of the land.”

The penalty applies to everyone. “A stranger” living among Israel and “a native of the land” are under the same law. Those who belong to Israel’s community keep the same feast.

20.brief: Israel is to eat nothing leavened but only unleavened bread in all their dwellings. The instructions about the feast close with a clear summary.
20.explain:
“You shall eat nothing leavened; in all your dwellings you shall eat unleavened bread.”

The instructions close with a summary. Israel is to eat “nothing leavened” in any of their homes during the feast.

21.brief: Moses calls the elders of Israel and tells them to choose lambs for their families and kill the Passover. Moses passes God’s instructions to Israel’s leaders, who will carry them out in every household.
21.explain:
“Then Moses called for all the elders of Israel and said to them,”

Moses passes God’s words on to “all the elders of Israel,” the leaders of the families and tribes.

“Pick out and take lambs for yourselves according to your families, and kill the Passover lamb.”

The elders are to have each family choose a lamb and “kill the Passover lamb.” Moses gives Israel’s leaders the instructions, and they will see that every household carries them out.

22.brief: The people are to dip a bunch of hyssop in the blood, strike the lintel and doorposts, and stay inside until morning. The people must remain under the protection of the blood all night.
22.explain:
“And you shall take a bunch of hyssop,”

Moses adds a detail. The blood is to be applied with “a bunch of hyssop,” a small plant with leafy branches that could hold liquid.

“dip it in the blood that is in the basin, and strike the lintel and the two doorposts with the blood that is in the basin.”

The hyssop is dipped in the blood and used to mark the door.

“And none of you shall go out of the door of his house until morning.”

No one is to leave the house until morning. The people must remain under the protection of the blood all night.
22.notes:
Hyssop was later used in cleansing rites (Leviticus 14:4–7; Numbers 19:18). David prays, “Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean” (Psalm 51:7). The exact plant is uncertain.

The Hebrew word translated “basin” can also mean “threshold.” Some understand the lamb to have been killed at the doorway, with the blood collecting at the threshold.

23.brief: When the LORD passes through to strike the Egyptians and sees the blood, He will pass over the door and not allow “the destroyer” to enter their houses. The blood is the sign of God’s protection against the judgment that falls on Egypt.
23.explain:
“For the LORD will pass through to strike the Egyptians;”

God Himself will “pass through” to bring judgment on Egypt.

“and when He sees the blood on the lintel and on the two doorposts, the LORD will pass over the door”

When God sees the blood, He will “pass over the door.” The blood marks the house as protected.

“and not allow the destroyer to come into your houses to strike you.”

God will “not allow the destroyer” to enter. “The destroyer” is the agent of God’s judgment that night. The LORD Himself guards the door marked with blood. The blood is the sign of God’s protection against the judgment that falls on Egypt.
23.notes: Hebrews 11:28 says that by faith Moses “kept the Passover and the sprinkling of blood, lest he who destroyed the firstborn should touch them.” Scripture elsewhere speaks of a destroying angel carrying out God’s judgment (2 Samuel 24:16; 1 Chronicles 21:15).

24.brief: Israel is to observe this as an ordinance for themselves and their sons forever. The Passover is not only for this night but for all their generations.
24.explain:
“And you shall observe this thing as an ordinance for you and your sons forever.”

The Passover is not only for this one night. It is “an ordinance for you and your sons forever.” Each generation is to keep it.

25.brief: When they come into the land the LORD promised, they are to keep this service. Moses speaks of the land as certain, so the command assumes God will finish what He has begun.
25.explain:
“It will come to pass when you come to the land which the LORD will give you, just as He promised, that you shall keep this service.”

Moses speaks of the land as certain. “When you come to the land.” Israel has not yet left Egypt, but the command assumes they will enter Canaan. God will finish what He has begun, “just as He promised.”
25.notes: The Hebrew word translated “service” is the same word used for Israel’s hard “bondage” in Egypt (1:14; 6:6, 9). Israel moves from forced service to Pharaoh to worshipful service to the LORD.

26.brief: Their children will ask, “What do you mean by this service?” God expects the observance to prompt questions that open the way for teaching the next generation.
26.explain:
“And it shall be, when your children say to you, ‘What do you mean by this service?”

God expects children to ask about the meal. The unusual customs, the lamb, the bitter herbs, the unleavened bread, would prompt questions. Their questions would open the way for teaching the next generation.

27.brief: Parents are to answer that it is the Passover sacrifice of the LORD, who passed over Israel’s houses and delivered their households, and the people bow their heads and worship. Israel responds to God’s instructions with worship before the deliverance has even happened.
27.explain:
“that you shall say, ‘It is the Passover sacrifice of the LORD,”

Parents are to explain that the meal is “the Passover sacrifice of the LORD.” It belongs to Him.

“who passed over the houses of the children of Israel in Egypt when He struck the Egyptians and delivered our households.”

The answer tells what God did. He “passed over” Israel’s houses, “struck the Egyptians,” and “delivered our households.” Each generation is to speak of it as their own deliverance: “our households.”

“So the people bowed their heads and worshiped.”

The people respond with worship. They “bowed their heads and worshiped” before the deliverance had even happened. They believed God’s promise, as they had when Moses first came (4:31).

28.brief: The children of Israel go and do just as the LORD commanded Moses and Aaron. The people obey God’s word fully.
28.explain:
“Then the children of Israel went away and did so; just as the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron, so they did.”

Israel obeyed fully. They did “just as the LORD had commanded.” Their worship was followed by obedience.

29.brief: At midnight the LORD strikes every firstborn in Egypt, from Pharaoh’s firstborn on the throne to the firstborn of the captive in the dungeon, and the firstborn of livestock. God carries out the judgment exactly as He announced.
29.explain:
“And it came to pass at midnight that the LORD struck all the firstborn in the land of Egypt,”

At “midnight” the judgment fell, as God had said (11:4). “The LORD struck all the firstborn.”

“from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sat on his throne to the firstborn of the captive who was in the dungeon,”

The judgment reached from the palace to the prison. Pharaoh’s heir and the son of a prisoner in “the dungeon” both died. In 11:5 the lowest rank was the servant at the handmill. Here it is the captive in the dungeon. Both phrases show that no level of Egyptian society escaped.

“and all the firstborn of livestock.”

The firstborn of the animals died too, as announced (11:5).

30.brief: Pharaoh, his servants, and all Egypt rise in the night, and there is a great cry, “for there was not a house where there was not one dead.” The grief reaches every Egyptian home, including the palace.
30.explain:
“So Pharaoh rose in the night, he, all his servants, and all the Egyptians;”

Pharaoh and all Egypt woke in the night. The king was not spared the grief.

“and there was a great cry in Egypt, for there was not a house where there was not one dead.”

The “great cry” foretold in 11:6 rose across the land. “There was not a house where there was not one dead.” The grief reached every Egyptian home, including the palace.

31.brief: Pharaoh calls Moses and Aaron by night and tells them to rise, go out, and “serve the LORD as you have said.” After all his refusals, Pharaoh now commands Israel to leave on God’s terms.
31.explain:
“Then he called for Moses and Aaron by night, and said,”

Pharaoh summons Moses and Aaron that same night. He sends for them himself.

“Rise, go out from among my people, both you and the children of Israel.”

Pharaoh now commands what he refused so long. “Rise, go out.” Everyone is to leave.

“And go, serve the LORD as you have said.”

Pharaoh gives in on every point. They may serve the LORD on the terms Moses gave. The terms are now God’s, not Pharaoh’s.

32.brief: Pharaoh tells them to take their flocks and herds as they asked and adds, “and bless me also.” The king who resisted the LORD now asks for a blessing from His servants.
32.explain:
“Also take your flocks and your herds, as you have said, and be gone;”

The animals may go too, “as you have said.” Pharaoh’s last condition (10:24) is gone.

“and bless me also.”

Pharaoh adds a request: “bless me also.” The king who resisted the LORD now asks for a blessing from the LORD’s servants. He recognizes, at least for this moment, that blessing comes through them.

33.brief: The Egyptians urge the people to leave quickly, saying, “We shall all be dead.” Egypt’s fear now drives Israel out, just as God said in Exodus 11:1.
33.explain:
“And the Egyptians urged the people, that they might send them out of the land in haste.”

The Egyptians press Israel to leave “in haste.” God had said Pharaoh would drive them out (11:1).

“For they said, ‘We shall all be dead.”

Fear drives the Egyptians. “We shall all be dead.” Egypt’s fear now drives Israel out, just as God said.

34.brief: The people take their dough before it is leavened, with their kneading bowls bound in their clothes on their shoulders. Their haste explains why the bread of the feast is unleavened.
34.explain:
“So the people took their dough before it was leavened,”

The people leave so quickly that their dough has no time to rise. They take it “before it was leavened.”

“having their kneading bowls bound up in their clothes on their shoulders.”

They wrap their “kneading bowls” in their cloaks and carry them on their shoulders. Their haste explains why the bread of the feast is unleavened.

35.brief: The children of Israel had done as Moses said and asked the Egyptians for articles of silver, gold, and clothing. Israel obeyed the instruction God gave in Exodus 11:2.
35.explain:
“Now the children of Israel had done according to the word of Moses,”

Israel had followed Moses’ instructions given in 11:2.

“and they had asked from the Egyptians articles of silver, articles of gold, and clothing.”

They “asked” for silver, gold, and clothing, as God commanded (3:22; 11:2).

36.brief: The LORD gave the people favor with the Egyptians, who gave them what they asked, “Thus they plundered the Egyptians.” The Egyptians freely gave these goods because the LORD gave Israel favor, fulfilling His promise in Exodus 3:21–22.
36.explain:
“And the LORD had given the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians, so that they granted them what they requested.”

The Egyptians gave freely because “the LORD had given the people favor.” God moved their hearts.

“Thus they plundered the Egyptians.”

The word “plundered” pictures the spoil an army takes from a defeated enemy. Israel took no spoil by force. The Egyptians gave freely because the LORD gave Israel favor. After generations of unpaid labor, Israel left with the wealth of Egypt, as God promised (3:21–22; Genesis 15:14).
36.notes: Psalm 105:37 says God “brought them out with silver and gold.” Exodus later records gold given for the tabernacle (35:22–24) and gold earrings used to make the calf (32:2–4). Those passages do not trace individual items back to the Egyptians, though a connection with the wealth received here is plausible.

37.brief: The children of Israel journey from Rameses to Succoth, about six hundred thousand men on foot, besides children. The family of seventy has become a great people setting out from Egypt.
37.explain:
“Then the children of Israel journeyed from Rameses to Succoth,”

The journey begins. Israel sets out “from Rameses,” one of the store cities they had built (1:11), “to Succoth.”

“about six hundred thousand men on foot, besides children.”

The number given is “about six hundred thousand men on foot,” not counting women and children. The family of seventy who came to Egypt (1:5) has become a great people. The text records this figure as written, and it agrees with later counts (Numbers 1:46; 11:21).
37.notes:
The passage gives only the count of men on foot, besides children. Any total for the whole company, including women and children, is an estimate that depends on assumptions the passage does not supply. Some interpreters propose that the Hebrew word for “thousand” here means a clan or military unit, which would make the number much smaller. That reading is not followed here, since the census totals in Numbers add up as thousands.

The location of Succoth is uncertain. It is often identified with a site in the eastern Nile Delta.

38.brief: A mixed multitude goes up with them, along with flocks, herds, and a great deal of livestock. Others besides Israel leave Egypt with them, and they take their animals as Moses insisted.
38.explain:
“A mixed multitude went up with them also,”

“A mixed multitude” left with Israel. These were people of other backgrounds, perhaps Egyptians and other foreigners who had seen the LORD’s power and chose to go with His people.

“and flocks and herds—a great deal of livestock.”

Israel left with “a great deal of livestock,” just as Moses insisted (10:26).
38.notes: Numbers 11:4 speaks of “the mixed multitude” among those who complained in the wilderness, and that group is often associated with the one here. The NKJV uses the same English expression in both places, but the passages do not establish that the two groups are identical. The Passover law in 12:48 makes provision for outsiders who join themselves to Israel.

39.brief: The people bake unleavened cakes from the dough they brought out, because they were driven out and had no time to prepare provisions. The unleavened bread remembers the haste of the departure.
39.explain:
“And they baked unleavened cakes of the dough which they had brought out of Egypt;”

On the way, the people baked “unleavened cakes” from the dough they had carried (12:34).

“for it was not leavened, because they were driven out of Egypt and could not wait, nor had they prepared provisions for themselves.”

The bread was unleavened because they “were driven out” and had no time. The unleavened bread of the feast would remind every generation of the haste of that night.

40.brief: “Now the sojourn of the children of Israel who lived in Egypt was four hundred and thirty years.” The verse records the length of Israel’s sojourn as the long period of waiting comes to an end.
40.explain:
“Now the sojourn of the children of Israel who lived in Egypt was four hundred and thirty years.”

The narrator records the length of Israel’s stay: “four hundred and thirty years.” The long period of waiting has come to an end. God told Abraham his descendants would be afflicted for four hundred years (Genesis 15:13), a round figure that fits this total.
40.notes: Interpreters understand the 430 years in two main ways. Many take them as the time Israel spent in Egypt itself, from Jacob’s arrival to the exodus, which fits Genesis 15:13 and Acts 7:6. Others count from Abraham’s arrival in Canaan, combining the time in Canaan and Egypt. This view follows Galatians 3:17, which places the law 430 years after the promise, and the Greek and Samaritan texts of this verse, which add “and in the land of Canaan.” The four generations of Genesis 15:16 and the genealogy in Exodus 6:16–20 are discussed on both sides. The NKJV text of this verse speaks of the sojourn of the children of Israel who lived in Egypt.

41.brief: At the end of the four hundred and thirty years, “on that very same day,” all the armies of the LORD go out from Egypt. God brings His people out at the exact time He appointed.
41.explain:
“And it came to pass at the end of the four hundred and thirty years—on that very same day—”

The departure came “on that very same day,” exactly at the end of the 430 years. God was not late.

“it came to pass that all the armies of the LORD went out from the land of Egypt.”

Israel is called “the armies of the LORD.” They leave not as escaping slaves but as the LORD’s people marching out in ordered ranks. God brings His people out at the exact time He appointed.

42.brief: The night is “a night of solemn observance to the LORD” for bringing them out, to be kept by all Israel throughout their generations. The LORD kept watch over Israel that night, and Israel is to keep this night for Him.
42.explain:
“It is a night of solemn observance to the LORD for bringing them out of the land of Egypt.”

The night is “a night of solemn observance to the LORD.” The phrase can mean a night of watching. The LORD kept watch over Israel that night as He brought them out.

“This is that night of the LORD, a solemn observance for all the children of Israel throughout their generations.”

Now Israel is to keep watch for Him. “That night of the LORD” is to be observed by every generation. The LORD kept watch over Israel that night, and Israel is to keep this night for Him.
42.notes: The Hebrew phrase translated “night of solemn observance” reads literally night of watchings. The same word appears twice in the verse, once for the LORD’s watching and once for Israel’s.

43.brief: The LORD gives Moses and Aaron the ordinance of the Passover: “No foreigner shall eat it.” The meal belongs to those who are part of God’s covenant people.
43.explain:
“And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, ‘This is the ordinance of the Passover:”

God gives further rules for the Passover, this time about who may eat it.

“No foreigner shall eat it.”

“No foreigner” may eat the Passover. The word refers to an outsider who has not joined Israel’s covenant. The meal belongs to those who are part of God’s covenant people.

44.brief: A servant bought with money may eat it once he has been circumcised. Through the covenant sign, those who join Israel’s households may share in the Passover.
44.explain:
“But every man’s servant who is bought for money, when you have circumcised him, then he may eat it.”

A servant “bought for money” belonged to an Israelite household. Once “circumcised,” he could share in the Passover. Through the covenant sign, those who join Israel’s households may take part in the meal.
44.notes: Circumcision was the sign of God’s covenant with Abraham, given for every male in the household, including servants bought with money (Genesis 17:12–13).

45.brief: A sojourner or a hired servant may not eat it. Temporary residents and hired workers who have not joined the covenant people are excluded.
45.explain:
“A sojourner and a hired servant shall not eat it.”

“A sojourner” here means a temporary resident, and “a hired servant” a worker paid by the day. These had not joined the covenant people and could not eat the Passover.
45.notes: The Hebrew word translated “sojourner” in this verse differs from the word translated “stranger” in 12:48–49. The “stranger” in 12:48 is a resident outsider who chooses to join Israel through circumcision.

46.brief: The Passover is to be eaten in one house, none of the meat carried outside, “nor shall you break one of its bones.” The lamb is kept whole, and John 19:36 sees this fulfilled in Christ’s death.
46.explain:
“In one house it shall be eaten; you shall not carry any of the flesh outside the house,”

The lamb is eaten “in one house.” None of the meat may be taken outside. The household that shelters under the blood eats the lamb together.

“nor shall you break one of its bones.”

The lamb’s bones must not be broken. The lamb is kept whole.
46.notes: John records that the soldiers did not break Jesus’ legs on the cross, and he sees this as fulfilling the Scripture, “Not one of His bones shall be broken” (John 19:36; compare Numbers 9:12; Psalm 34:20).

47.brief: All the congregation of Israel shall keep it. The Passover is required of the whole people, not only some families.
47.explain:
“All the congregation of Israel shall keep it.”

The Passover is required of “all the congregation of Israel.” It is not optional. The whole people is to keep it.

48.brief: A stranger who wants to keep the Passover must have all his males circumcised, and then he may keep it as a native of the land, for no uncircumcised person may eat it. The door is open to outsiders who join themselves to the LORD through the covenant sign.
48.explain:
“And when a stranger dwells with you and wants to keep the Passover to the LORD,”

God makes provision for “a stranger” who lives among Israel and “wants to keep the Passover.” An outsider may come in by choice.

“let all his males be circumcised, and then let him come near and keep it;”

The way in is circumcision. All the males of his household must be “circumcised.” Then he may “come near and keep it.”

“and he shall be as a native of the land. For no uncircumcised person shall eat it.”

Once circumcised, he is “as a native of the land.” He stands with Israel as one of them. The door is open to outsiders who join themselves to the LORD through the covenant sign, but “no uncircumcised person shall eat it.”

49.brief: “One law shall be for the native-born and for the stranger who dwells among you.” Those who join Israel receive the same law and the same place at the Passover.
49.explain:
“One law shall be for the native-born and for the stranger who dwells among you.”

“One law” applies to both “the native-born” and “the stranger.” Those who join Israel receive the same law and the same place at the Passover.
49.notes: The same principle of one law for native and stranger appears elsewhere in the law (Leviticus 24:22; Numbers 9:14; 15:15–16).

50.brief: All the children of Israel do as the LORD commanded Moses and Aaron. The people again obey God’s instructions completely.
50.explain:
“Thus all the children of Israel did; as the LORD commanded Moses and Aaron, so they did.”

Israel again obeyed completely, as in 12:28. They did “as the LORD commanded.”

51.brief: On that very same day the LORD brings the children of Israel out of Egypt according to their armies. The chapter ends with the deliverance God promised accomplished by His own hand.
51.explain:
“And it came to pass, on that very same day, that the LORD brought the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt according to their armies.”

The chapter ends with the deliverance accomplished. “The LORD brought the children of Israel out.” It happened “on that very same day,” and they went out “according to their armies,” in ordered companies. The deliverance God promised has been accomplished by His own hand.
